newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Czech Union bank eyes stake in Bulgaria Hebrosbank.
newsitem.headline: Czech Union bank eyes stake in Bulgaria Hebrosbank.

text.p: The Czech Republic's Union bank was interested in acquiring a stake in Bulgaria's state-owned Hebrosbank, an official said on Tuesday.

"The Union bank has submitted a letter of intent, expressing interest in buying a stake in Hebrosbank," Bulgaria's Bank Consolidation Company (BCC) acting executive director Dimitar Dimitrov told Reuters.

A privatisation scheme for the Plovdiv-based bank and tender conditions will be offered to all interested investors by end-August so that the sell-off could be completed by the end of 1997, Dimitrov said.
Under pledges to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) Bulgaria is expected to privatise all of its six operating state-owned banks by mid-1998.
The BCC, which manages state equity in Bulgarian commercial banks, holds 97.5 percent of Hebrosbank capital totalling 10.5 billion levs.

In a bid to prepare the bank's privatisation more efficiently a shareholders' meeting on Tuesday elected a new three-member supervisory board, including deputy Industry Minister Marin Marinov, Milan Nikolov and Maria Koleva.
So far the supervisory board comprised the BCC as a legal entity, Krassimir Stoyanov and Anton Velichkov.
The BCC was replaced on the supervisory board in line with a new banking law requirement, banning legal entities from standing on bank management bodies.
Hebrosbank was back in profit last year with 2.02 million levs net after a 255.2 million lev loss for 1995.
The net profit will be transferred into the bank's reserves under a shareholders' decision, Dimitrov said.

The bank pre-tax profit for 1996 totalled 48.606 billion levs, of which 46.6 billion levs were set aside as provisions against risk assets and 113.630 million levs of taxes were paid, the bank's annual report showed.
Hebrosbank assets totalled 119.294 billion levs at the end of last year and its capital-to-risk assets ratio was 19.27 percent.
The bank's net worth totalled 1.416 billion levs at the end of 1996 after being negative the year before, an audit by Deloitte & Touche showed in March.

The rise in the net worth was due to a recapitalisation through domestic debt bonds worth $51 in July last year and the seven-fold lev fall against the dollar last year, because some 63 percent of the bank's assets were denominated in foreign currency and outweighed its dollar-denominated liabilities.
